10 units, each with key ideas, worked examples, a 10-mark exam-style question, common mistakes and quick recall

How this book matches your exam. Research check: this book follows the Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 syllabus (2026–2028 version). The six content areas are:

  1. Motion, forces and energy
  2. Thermal physics
  3. Waves
  4. Electricity and magnetism
  5. Nuclear physics
  6. Space physics

The assessment objectives are weighted 50% knowledge with understanding, 30% handling information and problem solving, and 20% experimental skills and investigations. You take a multiple-choice paper, a theory paper and a practical paper or an alternative-to-practical paper, at Core or Extended level (Extended content is called "Supplement" in the syllabus). The paper numbers, durations and marks are set out in Book 10; check them against the current syllabus.

This book covers topics 1.1 to 1.4: physical quantities and measurement, motion, mass and weight, and density. Supplement-only content is marked (S). In this book, take g = 9.8 N/kg (9.8 m/s²), as Cambridge papers do. Every answer was checked by computer. The marking guides are our own, not official Cambridge mark schemes.

Unit 1 of 10: Physical Quantities, Units and Measurement

Key ideas

  • SI base units: metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A), kelvin (K).
  • Prefixes: kilo (k, ×10³), centi (c, ×10⁻²), milli (m, ×10⁻³), micro (μ, ×10⁻⁶), mega (M, ×10⁶).
  • Measuring instruments: rulers (to 1 mm), measuring cylinders (read at the bottom of the meniscus, at eye level), stopwatches, balances.
  • Measuring small or fast quantities: time many oscillations and divide; measure the thickness of a stack of sheets and divide.

Worked examples

Example 1: a pendulum takes 32.4 s for 20 oscillations. Period = 32.4 ÷ 20 = 1.62 s.

Example 2: 500 sheets of paper are 5.0 cm thick. One sheet = 5.0 ÷ 500 = 0.010 cm (0.10 mm).

Example 3: 2.5 km = 2500 m; 350 g = 0.35 kg; 45 ms = 0.045 s.

10-mark exam-style question

(a) Write down the SI units of mass, time and length. [3]

(b) Convert 7.2 km to m and 850 mm to m. [2]

(c) Describe how to measure the period of a pendulum accurately. [3]

(d) Why is it better to time 20 oscillations rather than one? [2]

Answers: (a) kg, s, m. (b) 7200 m; 0.85 m. (c) Time 20 oscillations with a stopwatch; start timing at the centre of the swing (or use a fiducial marker); divide the total time by 20; repeat and average (B3). (d) The human reaction time error is shared over many oscillations, so the percentage error is much smaller (B2).

Common mistakes

  1. Reading a measuring cylinder at the top of the meniscus. 2. Timing one oscillation. 3. Prefix errors (m for milli versus M for mega). 4. No units in answers. 5. Parallax errors from viewing at an angle.

Quick recall

  1. SI unit of current? 2. 1 mm in m? 3. Where do you read a meniscus? 4. What does μ mean? 5. Period of 10 oscillations taking 15 s?

Answers: 1) Ampere. 2) 0.001 m. 3) At the bottom, at eye level. 4) ×10⁻⁶. 5) 1.5 s.
